doc.title: Von Freeman — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

chapter: Bird, Ben Webster and the 1950s decline
title: Miles Davis from the cool to the electric band
summary: He recalls progressive jazz, then a Miles gig where he emceed, with Cicely Tyson in the wings, and the electric music.

story.theme_name: Playing with and around Miles Davis
story.community_name: Playing with Miles Davis: joining, sessions and the band

blocks.x: That’s right. So the masses of people that were behind bebop and whatnot – of course Miles [Davis] got in there and saved a little something, because he and Gerry Mulligan put out progressive music. So instead of calling it bebop . . .
Birth of the Cool and all that.
. . . they called it progressive. Yeah, Birth of the Cool. Then when Miles decided to go into his other thing, that was like . . .

Yeah, because a lot of cats – like, I was working clubs. Cats were saying, “He’s on it. But what’s that that you’re playing?” They say, “Why don’t you . . . ? – you can’t be hipper than Miles Davis.” Miles was playing what they thought was like rock or something. So I said, aw, Miles, come on. Come back to jazz. Because one night I emceed for Miles, one of Miles’s groups. Boy, they were paying him a lot of money. He made all the money [?], and he’s playing this music. I’m looking at this great man playing this music. He was with – what was the real – the art woman that he was married to for about . . . ?

Yeah. She’s sitting over in the wings. You know how Miles used to act. He had a different act altogether. He was playing like nursery rhymes [Freeman sings a ditty]. Then he’d smile at her. “Come on, give us some sugar” or something. Then he – and something was wrong with his leg.
And man, he was tearing the house up with this music. Of course all the diehards were sitting there, “Aw man, aw man.” But the people were going crazy.
It was a whole different set of people.
Yeah, what I’m trying to tell you. What he had going, he had going. He had the guitar players, was outside. They was . . .
He had a cat from here for a while. What’s his name?
I just talked to him a week ago or two. I’ll never think of his name.
Yeah, he was [Freeman makes a warbling sound]. He had two or three drummers.
Jack [DeJohnette] played with him in that period.

He had an organ setup, and every now and then he’d go and he’d play some chords. He’d do something. I’d say, well Miles, I, goodness – but I could see where he was getting over. But I was used to that other Miles, the one that was burning.
